newsitem.title: INDIA: India PM warned off populist budget after rout.
newsitem.headline: India PM warned off populist budget after rout.

text.p: Humbling defeats for India's ruling centre-left alliance in key local polls could tempt it to staunch the slide with a populist budget this month, but rival parties said on Wednesday that such a move would be disastrous.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party lost the legislature seat he vacated in his home state of Karnataka, and two leftist allies of the ruling United Front coalition were humbled in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Punjab.

At the same time, analysts said, Deve Gowda's position had been bolstered by embarrassing defeats for the Congress party, Deve Gowda's reluctant ally in parliament, in parliamentary and local by-elections in four key northern states.
"The Congress is not politically in a position to disturb us," Janata Dal deputy Wasim Ahmed told Reuters. "But we, too, must act to win back the support of the people, particularly the poor masses."
Left-wing groups within the United Front said they expect the government to announce steps to help ease the rising cost of living, especially for food and petroleum products.
The government has postponed a widely expected announcement to cut hefty state subsidies on petrol until after the budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year is unveiled on February 28.

"For populism you need money, and you don't have that luxury at your disposal," said Jaswant Singh, a former federal finance minister and leader of the opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the biggest group in parliament.
"If there is a populist budget, it would be an act of great criminality," Singh warned.

The right-wing BJP and its Sikh allies routed the Congress and the United Front in state legislature polls in Punjab last week. The BJP also scored major successes against the Congress Party and Deve Gowda's alliance in several other assembly and parliamentary by-elections this week.

The Congress, which suffered its worst-ever defeat in last year's general elections, has frequently threatened to bring down Deve Gowda's government for what it says is political and economic mismanagement.
On Wednesday, though, it was licking its own wounds.
Congress strategists said the party's image had been badly dented by corruption scandals involving its senior leaders.

Also, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), probing a controversial $1.3 billion howitzer gun deal in 1986, on Tuesday disclosed the names of five people it said had received payments from Swedish arms manufacturer Bofors AB.
The furore over the suspected payments contributed to the 1989 defeat of the Congress government led by Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
Gandhi, who was assassinated in 1991, strenuously denied the allegations. On Tuesday, Congress spokesman Tariq Anwar repeated that neither Gandhi nor his family members were involved.
"We do not want an early election," Congress spokesman Ved Prakash told Reuters, a day after the disastrous election results and the CBI's revelations.

"But that does not mean that the government should take our support for granted," Prakash said. "We do not want them to play tricks with the budget. If they do bring a populist package, people will see through that."
